title: Defining ratios in the Cartesian plane

sections.title: Defining ratios in the Cartesian plane

subtopics.title: Angle from point coordinates
subtopics.exposition: The angle between the line from the origin to a point and the positive x-axis is said to be in the standard position of an angle (for Q(-2, 3), angle B is this angle). To find the angle for a plotted point, draw a line from the origin to the point and draw a dotted line from the point to the x-axis, so that a right-angled triangle is constructed. The coordinates of the point give the sides of the triangle: for P(2, 3), x = 2 and y = 3, so the side opposite angle A has length 3 and the adjacent side has length 2. With the opposite side 3 and the adjacent side 2, use tan A = opposite/adjacent = 3/2 to calculate A = 56.3 degrees. Alternatively, use the theorem of Pythagoras to calculate the hypotenuse of the triangle and then calculate the angle using sin A = opposite/hypotenuse or cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse. For a point in the second quadrant such as Q(-2, 3), let alpha be the angle between line OQ and the negative x-axis, so that B + alpha = 180 degrees. From the coordinates of Q(-2, 3), the side opposite alpha has length 3 and the adjacent side has length 2. Use tan alpha = opposite/adjacent = 3/2 to calculate alpha = 56.3 degrees, then the angle in standard position is B = 180 degrees - alpha = 123.7 degrees. Alternatively, calculate the hypotenuse using the theorem of Pythagoras and calculate alpha using sin alpha = opposite/hypotenuse or cos alpha = adjacent/hypotenuse. Angles are always measured from the positive x-axis in an anti-clockwise direction.

subtopics.title: Ratios of a point (x;y)
subtopics.exposition: The trigonometric ratios, first defined using right-angled triangles, extend to any angle; the definitions do not rely on the lengths of the sides of the triangle but on the size of the angle only. For a point P(x, y), a circle centred on the origin passing through P has radius r, which is the length from the origin to P. The angle between line OP and the x-axis is denoted theta. sin theta = y/r. cosec theta = r/y. cos theta = x/r. sec theta = r/x. tan theta = y/x. cot theta = x/y. To calculate the ratios for a point (x, y) without a calculator, use the theorem of Pythagoras to find r: r squared = x squared + y squared (for P(-3, 4), r squared = 25, so r = 5). After finding r, substitute the values of x, y and r into the required ratios (for P(-3, 4): x = -3, y = 4, r = 5). For P(-3, 4), cos theta = x/r = -3/5.

subtopics.title: Ratios from a given ratio and quadrant
subtopics.exposition: The letters C, A, S and T on the diagram of the quadrants indicate which of the ratios are positive in each quadrant. The diagram showing which ratios are positive in each quadrant is known as the CAST diagram. Quadrant I: both x and y are positive, so all ratios are positive. Quadrant II: y is positive, so sin and cosec are positive (they are defined in terms of y and r). Quadrant III: both x and y are negative, so tan and cot are positive (they are defined in terms of x and y). Quadrant IV: x is positive, so cos and sec are positive (they are defined in terms of x and r). tan squared theta + 1 = sec squared theta; the book proves it by substituting x = -5, y = -12 and r = 13 for a point in the third quadrant. Start by sketching the point in the Cartesian plane and labelling the angle. To find a missing coordinate, rearrange the theorem of Pythagoras: y squared = r squared - x squared (for r = 13 and x = -5, y squared = 144, so y = plus or minus 12). The quadrant decides the sign of the missing coordinate: given that theta lies in the third quadrant, y must be negative, so y = -12. To evaluate an expression such as 3 tan theta, replace the ratio with its definition in x, y and r and simplify: for P(-3, 4), 3 tan theta = 3(y/x) = 3(4/-3) = -4. To evaluate (1/2) cosec theta, replace cosec theta with r/y and simplify: for P(-3, 4), (1/2)(5/4) = 5/8. For a squared ratio, substitute x, y and r into the definition and square it: tan squared theta + 1 = (y/x) squared + 1, which for x = -5, y = -12 gives 144/25 + 1 = 169/25. The right-hand side is worked out separately: sec squared theta = (r/x) squared = (13/-5) squared = 169/25. To prove an identity for the point, work out the left-hand side and the right-hand side separately; when they are equal, the identity is proved. The Cartesian plane is divided into 4 quadrants in an anti-clockwise direction.

subtopics.title: Special angle ratio values
subtopics.exposition: When theta = 0 degrees, the length of the opposite side is 0 and the length of the adjacent side equals the length of the hypotenuse. When theta = 90 degrees, the length of the adjacent side is 0 and the length of the opposite side equals the length of the hypotenuse. sin 0 degrees = opposite/hypotenuse = 0/hypotenuse = 0. cos 0 degrees = adjacent/hypotenuse = hypotenuse/hypotenuse = 1. tan 0 degrees = opposite/adjacent = 0/adjacent = 0. sin 90 degrees = opposite/hypotenuse = hypotenuse/hypotenuse = 1. cos 90 degrees = adjacent/hypotenuse = 0/hypotenuse = 0. tan 90 degrees = opposite/adjacent = opposite/0, which is undefined. Special angle values of sin theta for 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees: 0, 1/2, 1/sqrt2, sqrt3/2, 1. Special angle values of cos theta for 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees: 1, sqrt3/2, 1/sqrt2, 1/2, 0. Special angle values of tan theta for 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees: 0, 1/sqrt3, 1, sqrt3, undefined. When working in the Cartesian plane, two other special angles are included in right-angled triangles: 0 degrees and 90 degrees.

The trigonometric ratios, first defined using right-angled triangles, extend to any angle; the definitions do not rely on the lengths of the sides of the triangle but on the size of the angle only.
The definitions of the reciprocal ratios (cosec, sec, cot) are extended to the Cartesian plane in the same way.
For a point P(x, y), a circle centred on the origin passing through P has radius r, which is the length from the origin to P.
The angle between line OP and the x-axis is denoted theta.
sin theta = y/r.
cosec theta = r/y.
cos theta = x/r.
sec theta = r/x.
tan theta = y/x.
cot theta = x/y.
To calculate the ratios for a point (x, y) without a calculator, use the theorem of Pythagoras to find r: r squared = x squared + y squared (for P(-3, 4), r squared = 25, so r = 5).
r is positive, as it is the radius of the circle.
After finding r, substitute the values of x, y and r into the required ratios (for P(-3, 4): x = -3, y = 4, r = 5).
For P(-3, 4), cos theta = x/r = -3/5.
The Cartesian plane is divided into 4 quadrants in an anti-clockwise direction.
r is always positive but x and y change with the position of the point, so the trigonometric ratios can be positive or negative.
The letters C, A, S and T on the diagram of the quadrants indicate which of the ratios are positive in each quadrant.
The diagram showing which ratios are positive in each quadrant is known as the CAST diagram.
Quadrant I: both x and y are positive, so all ratios are positive.
Quadrant II: y is positive, so sin and cosec are positive (they are defined in terms of y and r).
Quadrant III: both x and y are negative, so tan and cot are positive (they are defined in terms of x and y).
Quadrant IV: x is positive, so cos and sec are positive (they are defined in terms of x and r).
The hypotenuse, r, is a length, and is therefore always positive.
Whenever you have to solve trigonometric problems without a calculator, it can be very helpful to make a sketch.
Start by sketching the point in the Cartesian plane and labelling the angle.

The quadrant decides the sign of the missing coordinate: given that theta lies in the third quadrant, y must be negative, so y = -12.
To evaluate an expression such as 3 tan theta, replace the ratio with its definition in x, y and r and simplify: for P(-3, 4), 3 tan theta = 3(y/x) = 3(4/-3) = -4.
To evaluate (1/2) cosec theta, replace cosec theta with r/y and simplify: for P(-3, 4), (1/2)(5/4) = 5/8.
For a squared ratio, substitute x, y and r into the definition and square it: tan squared theta + 1 = (y/x) squared + 1, which for x = -5, y = -12 gives 144/25 + 1 = 169/25.
The right-hand side is worked out separately: sec squared theta = (r/x) squared = (13/-5) squared = 169/25.

tan squared theta + 1 = sec squared theta; the book proves it by substituting x = -5, y = -12 and r = 13 for a point in the third quadrant.
When working in the Cartesian plane, two other special angles are included in right-angled triangles: 0 degrees and 90 degrees.
When theta = 0 degrees, the length of the opposite side is 0 and the length of the adjacent side equals the length of the hypotenuse.
sin 0 degrees = opposite/hypotenuse = 0/hypotenuse = 0.
cos 0 degrees = adjacent/hypotenuse = hypotenuse/hypotenuse = 1.
tan 0 degrees = opposite/adjacent = 0/adjacent = 0.
When theta = 90 degrees, the length of the adjacent side is 0 and the length of the opposite side equals the length of the hypotenuse.
sin 90 degrees = opposite/hypotenuse = hypotenuse/hypotenuse = 1.
cos 90 degrees = adjacent/hypotenuse = 0/hypotenuse = 0.
tan 90 degrees = opposite/adjacent = opposite/0, which is undefined.
